A manufacturer that believes its customer is preparing to leave may claim ownership of molds and intellectual property, resurrect old debts, or threaten to stop production. For years, Chinese manufacturers faced intense price competition, weak demand in certain industries, and pressure from foreign buyers moving production elsewhere. In February 2024, Reuters published China's Tumbling Prices Push Some Exporters to the Brink. It described a Chinese lighting manufacturer that accepted a $1.5 million order at a price 25 percent below what it had charged for a similar order the previous year. For decades, people talked about "The China Price" to describe China's extraordinarily low manufacturing costs. I started calling situations like the one Reuters described as the China Desperation Price.
China's manufacturing economy has since changed. According to China's National Bureau of Statistics, producer prices rose 5 percent year over year in September 2026, while factories' input costs rose nearly 7 percent. Prices were still falling in some industries, including automobile manufacturing. Rising costs can make price cuts harder to get, but national statistics tell you little about what your own factory will charge. What we're seeing is that major manufacturers like Midea and Foxconn are thriving, while many smaller, less specialized factories are struggling. If you're a small company asking Midea for a price reduction, you have far less bargaining power than a company that buys 55 percent of a small factory's total annual production.
You also need to know why a factory is offering a reduction and whether it can afford the new price. A manufacturer with idle capacity might accept a smaller margin to keep its workers busy. Some factories agree to attractive prices and then substitute cheaper materials, delay production, or demand additional payments. A 20 percent price reduction won't help much if you end up with defective products or miss a major delivery deadline.
Tariffs have given American companies another reason to seek lower prices from Chinese manufacturers. When President Trump imposed heavy tariffs on Chinese products during his first administration, many American buyers asked their suppliers to absorb some of the additional expense. The same issue has arisen as U.S.-China tariff policies have continued changing. I've seen this approach work, particularly when the factory values the relationship and understands that higher import costs threaten future orders. Some manufacturers prefer a smaller margin to losing a good customer.

One company paid $80,000 for five molds used across three product lines. Manufacturers claim tooling was never fully paid for or demand additional compensation for development work, and some simply refuse to release it. Failing to register early can leave a foreign company fighting over a brand it has used for years. Some involved false claims, while others arose from disagreements over defective products or incomplete shipments.
If your manufacturer claims you owe money, or if you have unresolved disputes involving defective products, deposits, tooling, or previous orders, get those issues examined before you begin price negotiations. A factory willing to overlook a disputed invoice while receiving regular orders often becomes less accommodating when it believes those orders will stop.

My firm has represented foreign companies dealing with threats of violence, detention, and restrictions on leaving China. Official exit bans differ from detention or threats by private parties. When a company has a serious disagreement with a Chinese manufacturer, we generally advise against sending its executives to China to negotiate until we've assessed the risks. When companies contact us about negotiating lower manufacturing prices, they usually have a number in mind. I want to know that number, but I'm more interested in making sure that their legal and commercial position is well fortified first.
One factory demanded a 34 percent price increase, effective immediately, and the U.S. company on the receiving end came to us for help. We advised the company that suing to recover its molds would probably be slower and more expensive than making new ones. When the manufacturer wanted more money, it rejected the next purchase order. A price commitment that doesn't oblige the factory to supply products is not really a price commitment at all. An impressive-looking contract can be nearly worthless if it doesn't bind the Chinese factory controlling your production and assets.
Many years ago, an American company contacted us after learning that its $2 million order of Christmas tree lights would not be delivered when needed. We called the Chinese factory, which told us it had never heard of our client. It turned out the buyer had unknowingly been dealing through a sourcing agent that owed money to the factory. The factory had stopped production, and our client had to pay millions more to get its lights delivered. My law firm's China lawyers draft far more distribution agreements than they did a few years ago, and we rarely form Chinese companies for clients anymore. I estimate we helped set up more than 100 Chinese entities from 2005 to 2015 and fewer than ten over the next decade. Foreign companies still want Chinese customers, but many have lost their appetite for putting employees and substantial assets in China. A U.S. furniture manufacturer we represent wanted its American employees out of China, and it ended up selling its China business to the manager who ran it and financing most of the sale. I have favored using Chinese distributors for years, and I have watched Western companies spend a fortune trying to sell good products in China on their own, with disappointing results.
Selling in China is hard, and most of the clichés about doing business there have some truth to them. It is not one market, and you can do well in Shanghai and get nowhere in another city. A capable Chinese distributor knows the customers and has people on the ground to deal with the messiness of selling there, but the wrong one can tie up your market for years while selling almost nothing.
A distributor takes on much of the sales work and, depending on the agreement, after-sales support. The foreign supplier avoids the cost of a Chinese subsidiary and its employment, tax, and administrative obligations. Some of our clients have well-known products in China and no office or employees there. For other ways to reach Chinese customers without setting up a local company, see 6 Smart Strategies for Selling to China Without Being in China.
Using a distributor does not end the foreign supplier's China obligations. It still has to comply with Chinese product rules and protect its trademarks, and collecting from the distributor is its problem too. For many of our clients, the smaller physical presence is still worth a great deal, and keeping employees out of China also lowers the risk of exit bans arising from commercial disputes.
I start out skeptical of a distributor that approaches you first, because wanting your product says nothing about whether it can sell it. I want to know what a prospective distributor has actually sold, where it has sold it, and who buys from it. "National coverage" often turns out to mean a warehouse and two salespeople, so a company claiming a nationwide network ought to be able to name its salespeople and the customers they cover. Check its ownership and litigation history, and look hard at its finances, including whether it has the money to promote a new product or expects you to pay for the entire launch.
Experience with other foreign suppliers is useful, especially when those relationships have lasted. Ask for references and actually call them. Then ask my favorite question: How does our product fit with what you already sell? A distributor with complementary products can be an excellent choice. If it is making good money selling competing products, look much harder. Good China due diligence catches some of these problems before anyone signs.
Clients often bring us distribution agreements that have worked in Europe, the United States, or Australia. We use them as a starting point because they reflect how the client does business, but we almost always rewrite substantial parts of them for China, and the issues below are where most of that rewriting happens. We cover the questions we ask before drafting in China Distribution Contracts: The Questions We Ask.
The first question is who sells to the Chinese customer. A conventional distributor buys from the foreign supplier and resells on its own account. An agent finds customers and helps arrange sales for the supplier, usually for a commission. Our clients generally prefer the distributor model because the Chinese company takes direct responsibility for local sales and customer payments, and because it makes clear who handles importation.
Chinese law looks beyond what the contract calls the distributor to how the relationship actually works. A distributor that routinely signs contracts on your behalf can create Chinese tax exposure for you. Depending on the structure, the arrangement can also fall under China's franchise rules, which turn on how the business operates, including the rights the foreign supplier grants and the fees it collects.
I pay close attention to titles and authority. A distributor's key person often needs a serious title, such as China Director, to get meetings, above all with government buyers. We pair that title with a board-approved authorization letter that spells out exactly what the person can and cannot do on the client's behalf, for reasons we explain in Setting Up Your Chinese Distributor for Success: Titles and Authority Matter. The agreement needs to say whether the distributor can use sub-distributors and who answers for their conduct. Anti-bribery provisions belong here too. They matter most when the customers include state-owned enterprises or government bodies, and they need to address both Chinese law and, where it applies, the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
I have lost count of how many problems began with a foreign company assuming that its U.S. or European trademark registration protected it in China. China is primarily a first-to-file country. A distributor can apply to register your brand, and getting it back can be expensive. When a distributor has registered a client's mark, we can usually negotiate an assignment if the distributor wants to keep the relationship, and the odds improve when its real money comes from manufacturing the client's products for export. Refusals tend to come from distributors that do not make the products or that earn more using the brand in China themselves.
A Norwegian company once asked us about suing its former Chinese distributor, which was manufacturing and selling the Norwegian company's products in China. The company believed it owned the Chinese trademark. After all, the distributor had given it a registration certificate. The certificate was fake. The mark had been registered to a Chinese individual who was licensing it to the former distributor. What the company thought was a straightforward breach-of-contract claim had become a much harder case.
Register the mark in your company's own name before the distributor starts using your brand. At the very least, get your application on file first, though a pending application is not the equivalent of an issued registration. Choose your Chinese-language brand name yourself. If you leave that decision entirely to your distributor or the market, Chinese customers can end up knowing your product by a name someone else picked. Our China trademark registration guide explains the filing process, and China Trademarks and Your Chinese Distributor covers what a distributor can do to you by filing first.
We give the distributor only the trademark rights it needs to market and sell our client's products. Those rights end with the distribution agreement, subject to any agreed inventory sell-off rights. The distributor may not register the client's marks, Chinese names, logos, domains, or confusingly similar brands. Where a registered mark is licensed, we address recordal of the license with the Chinese trademark authorities. An unrecorded license is generally valid between the parties but cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties. If the distributor will receive valuable confidential information, we consider the protections in our China NNN agreement guide.
Before granting distribution rights, we check whether the product needs testing, certification, registration, Chinese labeling, or import permits. The agreement says who obtains and pays for each approval. If the distributor is responsible, we set a deadline and specify the consequences for missing it. Without that, a foreign supplier can wait indefinitely for sales that cannot legally begin.
I always want to know whose name will appear on each approval. An American medical device company we represented let its Chinese distributor act as its registration agent because the distributor offered to handle the paperwork at no charge. Five years later, the company wanted a stronger distributor. The old one was sitting on the registration certificate and the technical file and had no reason to cooperate. Every month it stalled was a month without sales. Where Chinese rules allow, we usually want the registration in our client's name.
The agreement specifies who handles warranty service and pays for recalls, including whether the supplier warrants directly to end customers or only to the distributor. Those provisions do not automatically shield the manufacturer from Chinese product-liability claims. If the distributor has few assets and inadequate insurance, its promise to indemnify the manufacturer is not worth much after a major product problem.
Chinese distributors often ask for nationwide exclusivity. We have seen companies sign five-year exclusive agreements and learn, two or three years in, that the distributor never placed a single order. The distributor signed to keep the product off the market while selling its own competing line, a pattern I describe in International Distribution Agreements: Beware the Eager Distributor. During the exclusive period, we generally bar the distributor from handling competing products, after checking that restriction against the competition law that applies.

China's rules effective February 1, 2026 provide only a narrow safe harbor for certain fixed or minimum resale-price restrictions. Even if those thresholds are met, the safe harbor does not apply where evidence shows the agreement eliminates or restricts competition.

None of our clients has ever had a real resale-price problem in China, but a number of distributors have threatened to sue our clients or report them to the authorities when relationships turned rocky, claiming minimum prices our clients never imposed. The agreements contained no price restrictions to support those threats. When resale price control matters to the business, we review the specific restriction and the law that applies before anyone signs. Form contracts imported from other countries cause enough trouble that we do not rely on whatever price clause the client's standard agreement contains.
I keep seeing the same fight start before a single order is placed. The supplier assumes the distributor will pay for advertising in exchange for exclusivity. The distributor expects the supplier to fund trade shows and provide samples, translations, and technical support. Nobody has worked out a budget. Six months later, both sides are annoyed, and sales have barely begun.
We try to settle who pays for what before we start drafting. If the distributor promises to translate manuals by a deadline or demonstrate the product to specified customers, we put those obligations in the agreement, along with our client's marketing commitments. A general promise to "promote the brand" is useless when the first year's sales come in far below expectations.
For a new distributor, I favor payment before shipment. After I wrote about selling into China without being there, two clients emailed me with the same advice. However you structure the deal, get paid enough up front to make it worth your while, because there is a very good chance you will never see another cent. Once the distributor establishes a payment history, a client may decide to offer 30-day terms. If it does, the agreement needs a way to return to advance payment when the distributor pays late or its finances deteriorate. We often put prices in a separate schedule, with a defined procedure for updating them, rather than locking prices into a long-term contract.
Shipping terms create avoidable disputes when the parties use familiar acronyms without understanding what they require, so identify the Incoterms rule and the named place. For many shipments, FCA (Free Carrier) makes more sense than EXW (Ex Works), which puts export clearance on the buyer even when that buyer is in China. For containerized freight, CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) often fits better than CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), which was designed for goods loaded on board a vessel.
A foreign supplier understandably wants the right to terminate when things go badly. I have seen draft agreements that allow termination for any reason on 90 days' notice, even though the distributor is expected to spend heavily developing the brand. Ask yourself why a serious distributor would agree to invest in a market it can lose after three months' notice. When a prospective distributor accepts those terms without a murmur, or never asks for automatic renewal once it hits its targets, I get suspicious about how much money it actually intends to spend. The contract term ought to reflect the product and the investment required. We start some relationships with a trial period and others with a longer term and regular purchase targets.
Unlike the law in some other countries, Chinese law generally does not give ordinary distributors a special statutory right to goodwill compensation simply because a distribution agreement ends. A foreign supplier that terminates in breach of its contract still faces a damages claim. A clause allowing termination for "breach" without specifying the grounds, notice requirements, or cure procedures leaves plenty to fight about when the parties disagree over what went wrong.
I distrust China contracts that read beautifully in English and provide for a lawsuit thousands of miles from the distributor's assets. For a mainland Chinese distributor, we ordinarily choose Chinese law and Chinese courts. Nearly all of our China contracts are bilingual, with Chinese as the controlling language. We never make both languages equally authoritative, because that invites an avoidable fight over what the parties agreed to.
When the defendant and its assets are in China, Chinese courts are generally the more direct and less expensive choice. I also think highly of CIETAC arbitration. State-owned enterprises often insist on it, and I prefer it when the distributor is in a smaller city where the local court is a concern. With CIETAC, freezing a distributor's assets still requires a Chinese court. We tend to leave the dispute-resolution provision until late in the drafting, and sometimes have two to five of our lawyers discuss jurisdiction and governing law before settling on it.
An English trading name and an informal signature do not establish which Chinese legal entity agreed to the deal. The agreement needs the distributor's correct registered Chinese legal name, and we normally also require its official company seal, or chop.
If a distributor registers our client's brand, sells outside its agreed territory, or keeps using the trademark after termination, our client needs a contract that clearly prohibits that conduct and provides a remedy that works under Chinese law. We frequently include contract damages provisions for those breaches. Those provisions can help define the monetary claim and support an application for property preservation, including a bank-account freeze. A damages clause does not freeze assets by itself. The court decides whether to grant preservation and can require security. Chinese companies generally understand what a damages clause can lead to in their own courts, which makes it one of the best tools we have for getting them to honor the contract. Pages of broad American-style indemnification language will not cure a contract that lacks usable remedies under Chinese law.
When a distribution relationship ends, the distributor is still holding whatever it has not sold. Without an agreed procedure, the parties fight over whether the distributor can sell the remaining inventory, whether the supplier must buy it back, and at what price. We answer those questions in the agreement, along with pending orders and continuing warranty obligations, while the two sides are still on speaking terms.
The foreign supplier needs some of the distributor's customer information to keep selling in China, even if the distributor built those customer relationships. Where those records contain personal information, China's Personal Information Protection Law governs how they are handled and when they can be sent outside China. The agreement must account for those limits instead of promising an unrestricted transfer. We establish who controls the Chinese websites, e-commerce storefronts, social media accounts, and domain names used to sell the brand. If a product approval cannot legally or practically be transferred, the contract needs realistic cooperation obligations rather than a meaningless promise to hand everything over.

For containerized freight, CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) often fits better than CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), which was designed for goods loaded on board a vessel.

8. A Good Distributor Needs Time to Build the Market

A foreign supplier understandably wants the right to terminate when things go badly. I have seen draft agreements that allow termination for any reason on 90 days' notice, even though the distributor is expected to spend heavily developing the brand. Ask yourself why a serious distributor would agree to invest in a market it can lose after three months' notice. When a prospective distributor accepts those terms without a murmur, or never asks for automatic renewal once it hits its targets, I get suspicious about how much money it actually intends to spend. The contract term ought to reflect the product and the investment required. We start some relationships with a trial period and others with a longer term and regular purchase targets.

Unlike the law in some other countries, Chinese law generally does not give ordinary distributors a special statutory right to goodwill compensation simply because a distribution agreement ends. A foreign supplier that terminates in breach of its contract still faces a damages claim. A clause allowing termination for "breach" without specifying the grounds, notice requirements, or cure procedures leaves plenty to fight about when the parties disagree over what went wrong.

9. Draft for Enforcement Against a Chinese Company

I distrust China contracts that read beautifully in English and provide for a lawsuit thousands of miles from the distributor's assets. For a mainland Chinese distributor, we ordinarily choose Chinese law and Chinese courts. Nearly all of our China contracts are bilingual, with Chinese as the controlling language. We never make both languages equally authoritative, because that invites an avoidable fight over what the parties agreed to.

When the defendant and its assets are in China, Chinese courts are generally the more direct and less expensive choice. I also think highly of CIETAC arbitration. State-owned enterprises often insist on it, and I prefer it when the distributor is in a smaller city where the local court is a concern. With CIETAC, freezing a distributor's assets still requires a Chinese court. We tend to leave the dispute-resolution provision until late in the drafting, and sometimes have two to five of our lawyers discuss jurisdiction and governing law before settling on it.

An English trading name and an informal signature do not establish which Chinese legal entity agreed to the deal. The agreement needs the distributor's correct registered Chinese legal name, and we normally also require its official company seal, or chop.

If a distributor registers our client's brand, sells outside its agreed territory, or keeps using the trademark after termination, our client needs a contract that clearly prohibits that conduct and provides a remedy that works under Chinese law. We frequently include contract damages provisions for those breaches. Those provisions can help define the monetary claim and support an application for property preservation, including a bank-account freeze. A damages clause does not freeze assets by itself. The court decides whether to grant preservation and can require security. Chinese companies generally understand what a damages clause can lead to in their own courts, which makes it one of the best tools we have for getting them to honor the contract. Pages of broad American-style indemnification language will not cure a contract that lacks usable remedies under Chinese law.

10. Plan the Breakup While the Relationship Is Still Good

When a distribution relationship ends, the distributor is still holding whatever it has not sold. Without an agreed procedure, the parties fight over whether the distributor can sell the remaining inventory, whether the supplier must buy it back, and at what price. We answer those questions in the agreement, along with pending orders and continuing warranty obligations, while the two sides are still on speaking terms.

The foreign supplier needs some of the distributor's customer information to keep selling in China, even if the distributor built those customer relationships. Where those records contain personal information, China's Personal Information Protection Law governs how they are handled and when they can be sent outside China. The agreement must account for those limits instead of promising an unrestricted transfer. We establish who controls the Chinese websites, e-commerce storefronts, social media accounts, and domain names used to sell the brand. If a product approval cannot legally or practically be transferred, the contract needs realistic cooperation obligations rather than a meaningless promise to hand everything over.

Check your deadlines immediately. The contract may require prompt notice of defects, provide a cure period, or set a deadline for arbitration. Statutory limitation periods vary by country and claim. Insurance claims, bank payment disputes, and marketplace procedures have their own deadlines. Two months of angry emails can cost a company an inexpensive remedy while it waits for a response that never comes.
Do not withhold payment or terminate the relationship without advice. Either step can trigger counterclaims or lead the supplier to hold back goods or tooling. With Chinese suppliers, unpaid invoices can also lead to a claim by Sinosure, China's export credit insurer. I would also resist the reflex to send a threatening lawyer letter. A demand can lead to settlement when the other side has money and wants to preserve the relationship. Control alone does not make a parent liable for its subsidiary's debts. Corporate records, contracts, bank instructions, registrations, and ownership information help establish who promised what and who owns the assets. A brand owner facing counterfeits may need an injunction. An investor forced out of a foreign joint venture may need access to company records before deciding whether to seek payment or negotiate an exit.
For straightforward litigation or arbitration in China, our usual screening threshold is about $350,000. Below that, we generally advise against proceeding because legal costs consume too much of the likely recovery. This is our practice threshold, not a Chinese legal minimum, and we do not apply it mechanically in other countries. Claims above $350,000 still need a viable defendant and realistic collection prospects.
The China monetary claims we prefer usually rest on contracts drafted for enforcement in China. We look for the registered Chinese name, proper company chop, a controlling Chinese-language version, and a defensible contract damages provision. Missing one of these does not defeat a claim. Chinese law also recognizes contracts formed through performance and electronic communications, so a plaintiff can establish contractual rights without a signed, chopped agreement. A smaller claim can still justify litigation when a factory is withholding essential tooling or an injunction can stop continuing harm. I have less enthusiasm for a large damages claim against a company with no reachable assets, however strong the liability evidence. The budget should cover appeals, enforcement, and the possibility that an asset search produces nothing. It should also address legal-fee recovery and, in some jurisdictions, the risk of paying some of the opposing party's costs if the client loses.
In South Korea, our lawyers obtained a court order freezing nearly $100 million in assets for American creditors, which led to a prompt, favorable settlement. Our foreign judgment enforcement work has also included securing a large seafood shipment in China belonging to a Danish company and using the threat of enforcement to recover helicopters in Papua New Guinea. Depending on the jurisdiction, a creditor can seek attachment, property preservation, a freezing injunction, or other temporary relief before the underlying case is decided. The applicant must meet local legal standards and may need to provide security, and an improper freeze can create liability. Some courts allow applications without advance notice when notice would defeat the order's purpose, and others impose stricter requirements.
Start with the contract. The governing-law clause identifies the substantive law the parties selected, subject to conflict-of-laws rules. The forum clause identifies the court they chose, while an arbitration clause sends covered disputes to arbitration. Choosing New York law in an English-language contract does not, by itself, give a New York court jurisdiction over every foreign defendant.
We have reviewed contracts that make an ordinary claim extraordinarily expensive to pursue. One agreement with a Chinese company required negotiation, followed by in-person mediation in China, followed by Chinese-language arbitration before three arbitrators, and the arbitrator-selection procedure was unclear as well. A straightforward payment claim under that agreement faced an expensive procedural path before anyone reached the merits.
I ordinarily remove mandatory negotiation and mediation requirements from our international contracts. Parties can negotiate or mediate whenever they wish, and we often recommend it. Mandatory steps give a party looking to delay another argument about why the case cannot proceed, sometimes while it moves assets. Carefully defined escalation procedures make sense in some transactions, but I do not insert them as boilerplate. We generally settle the dispute resolution clause near the end of contract drafting, after we understand the likely breaches, remedies, parties, and assets. Our article on Drafting China Dispute Resolution Clauses that Work discusses an actual contract illustrating the problem.
An unsigned or missing agreement complicates the forum question but does not necessarily defeat the claim. Purchase orders, payments, emails, and performance may establish a contract under the applicable law. The parties can still dispute whether an arbitration clause was accepted or a court has jurisdiction. Without an enforceable arbitration agreement, neither side can ordinarily force arbitration simply because it now prefers that forum. This is one reason the documents are the international deal.
To sue a foreign company in the United States, a plaintiff needs subject-matter jurisdiction, proper venue, and a valid basis for personal jurisdiction over the defendant. That basis may come from the defendant's relevant contacts with a state, its agreement to litigate there, or an applicable federal jurisdictional provision. American assets can help with collection, but owning them does not, by itself, establish personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. These questions need answers before filing.
American discovery attracts plaintiffs to U.S. courts, but obtaining evidence overseas can be difficult. Documents held by American banks and business partners may be accessible. Compelling testimony or records from a mainland Chinese company is another matter. China's evidence-gathering and data laws can restrict collection and transmission, and a U.S. subpoena is not directly enforceable in China. Before choosing an American forum, determine where the critical evidence is and whether you can obtain it.
Mainland China is a party to the Hague Service Convention and objects to the methods in Article 10, including postal service. When the Convention applies, service must follow a permitted method. For mainland Chinese defendants with known addresses, we generally recommend formal Hague service through the proper Convention channel, especially when the client may later seek recognition of the judgment in China. Service through China's Central Authority can take months and requires careful preparation, including translation.
Two recent federal appellate decisions make email service on defendants in China particularly risky. In Smart Study Co. v. Shenzhenshixindajixieyouxiangongsi, decided in December 2025, the Second Circuit held that the Hague Service Convention prohibited email service on the China-based defendants in that case. The Seventh Circuit adopted the same treaty interpretation in Kangol LLC v. Hangzhou Chuanyue Silk Import & Export Co. in May 2026, but remanded to determine whether the Convention applied given the dispute over the defendant's address. The defendant's actual location and the Convention's scope still matter. A quick default judgment obtained through questionable service is a poor bargain if it cannot later be enforced.
Suing in the defendant's home country can avoid a separate judgment-recognition proceeding when the local court can reach its assets. The challenge is local procedure. A case built around American depositions needs a different evidentiary approach in a court that relies mainly on documents.
For China manufacturing disputes, we often favor litigation in the right Chinese court when the defendant and its assets are in China. That court can enforce locally without first requiring recognition of an American judgment. Our experience with ordinary business disputes in major Chinese commercial centers has generally been favorable, though cases involving important local employers or politically sensitive interests require more caution.
Chinese courts can order property preservation when the applicable standards are met. A sensible contractual damages clause helps define the claim and can support a preservation application, but it does not automatically entitle the plaintiff to a bank freeze. The court decides whether to grant relief and may require security. Chinese manufacturers generally know that these clauses can lead to a frozen bank account, which makes a good damages provision one of the best ways to get a factory to honor its contract in the first place.

In qualifying arbitrations, parties can seek court-ordered property preservation, and the revised law also permits applications to a court in urgent situations before arbitration begins. We consider those remedies even when the contract requires arbitration.
CIETAC can be an excellent choice when a state-owned company insists on arbitration or there are reasons to avoid the defendant's local court. In a small city where the defendant is a major employer or taxpayer, properly structured arbitration may reduce concerns about local influence over the merits. The arbitral institution, seat, and available court assistance still matter.
When a dispute belongs in a Chinese court, we work with Chinese litigators we know. A foreign company hiring a Chinese law firm directly is almost always a mistake, because few foreign companies know China well enough to pick the right firm or to work with one on their own. International counsel helps select local lawyers, coordinate evidence and strategy, and keep the client informed about costs and risks. We take the same approach elsewhere, looking for lawyers who actually litigate in the relevant courts. A firm's claim that it handles international matters tells us little about its courtroom experience.
Arbitration has a genuine enforcement advantage when the debtor has assets in several countries. The New York Convention provides a system for recognizing and enforcing qualifying awards in more than 170 jurisdictions. It permits specified defenses to enforcement, but courts ordinarily do not retry the merits. No comparable worldwide system exists for ordinary foreign court judgments.
Arbitration can be expensive. Parties usually pay their lawyers, the administering institution, and the arbitrators. Three-member tribunals, experts, witnesses from different countries, translation, and hearings can push a substantial case into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Challenges to arbitral awards are tightly limited, and the losing party has little opportunity to correct an error.
As we discuss in our article on international arbitration in cross-border contracts, a contract binds only the parties covered by its arbitration agreement, subject to recognized rules concerning non-signatories. A dispute involving several affiliates and contracts can become procedurally difficult when only some parties agreed to arbitrate. Emergency arbitrators and court-assisted interim relief are available in certain arbitrations, but the powers and procedures vary.
Settlement becomes possible when the other side has a reason to make a deal. A supplier may want future orders. A debtor whose bank accounts have been frozen wants access to its money. Before negotiating, I want to know what the other side needs and what it can deliver. Repeating that our client has a strong case does little when the defendant thinks it can ignore us.
Mediation can work even in very large disputes. Our firm represented the Government of Haiti in a dispute with a Chinese construction company that ended in a private mediation settlement of nearly $35 million after approximately two years. Keep watching limitation periods and other deadlines while negotiations or mediation continue, and do not assume the discussions suspend them.
A settlement needs to be enforceable where performance is expected. Identify the actual obligated entity and any guarantors, address payment security and installments, and specify when claims are released. If a Chinese company is paying money or releasing goods in China, we usually want a Chinese-language agreement that works under Chinese law and before the likely enforcement court. In one cross-border credit dispute we wrote about, incomplete settlement documents helped turn an apparent resolution into further litigation.
A U.S. judgment ordinarily must be recognized under the law of the foreign country before the creditor can use local enforcement procedures. The defendant may raise objections concerning jurisdiction, service, finality, or public policy. Collection is then governed by the law where the assets are located. A creditor cannot simply present an American judgment to a foreign bank and demand payment.

Arbitral awards ordinarily follow a different recognition framework, including the New York Convention where applicable. Even after recognition, the creditor needs assets it can lawfully reach. I reassess the economics before filing and whenever the next stage, including enforcement, requires substantial expense.
In a Yiwu supplier fraud matter, a buyer paid about $177,000 to a Chinese intermediary for three shipments. The first, worth approximately $35,000, arrived. The other goods never left China. According to the buyer, the intermediary passed only a small portion of the payment to the manufacturer, then spent months claiming that goods were nearly finished or had shipped. The buyer even sent representatives to investigate, but the promised deliveries never materialized.
We recommended that the buyer retain a reputable Chinese lawyer experienced in economic-crime complaints to evaluate a police referral. The alleged failure to fund production, coupled with false shipment claims, warranted examining whether the conduct was intentional fraud. We could not promise the police would accept the case, because Chinese authorities can treat a failed commercial transaction as a civil dispute.
Do not threaten criminal prosecution to collect an ordinary commercial debt. That can create legal problems of its own. When the evidence genuinely suggests fraud, counsel should evaluate criminal reporting alongside the civil claims and deadlines. Banks, payment platforms, insurers, and marketplaces may also offer recovery options worth investigating before financing an international lawsuit.
Companies sometimes disregard a foreign court summons because they have no operations in the country, believe the plaintiff is bluffing, or think a judgment issued there cannot affect them. An arbitration notice can be dismissed just as casually. That is a serious gamble. A foreign court may proceed to a default judgment, and an arbitral tribunal can issue an award when a properly notified respondent refuses to participate. The plaintiff may later attempt enforcement wherever the defendant has assets.
When foreign legal papers arrive, preserve the record and have counsel calculate the response deadline immediately. The first review should cover jurisdiction, service or arbitral notice, contractual forum requirements, and whether an appearance or objection affects available defenses. Check insurance and indemnification rights, related proceedings, and possible counterclaims. An ill-considered response can waive defenses that would otherwise remain available.
We also defend companies and owners when foreign creditors seek recognition of judgments in the United States. Recognition of foreign-country money judgments here is primarily governed by state law, often through a version of the Uniform Foreign-Country Money Judgments Recognition Act. The creditor ordinarily has to establish that the judgment qualifies for recognition, and the debtor can raise permitted defenses, including jurisdictional or serious notice and due-process defects. A U.S. court does not normally reopen the foreign case just because the debtor thinks the foreign judge got the facts wrong.
These cases often turn on old records: who was served, whether the defendant appeared, whether it objected to jurisdiction, and what happened in the foreign proceeding. The defense must fit the recognition law of the U.S. state where the creditor filed. We represent both sides of these disputes, and our article on enforcing or challenging foreign judgments in the United States explains the available objections.
Some years ago, I came across an email from one of our international litigators to a client considering a lawsuit in a small emerging-market country. The client wanted to know whether the claim was worth pursuing and which local firm to hire. Our lawyer had listed the questions we planned to ask the firms under consideration. I still use much the same list today.
That last question matters most to me. I distrust lawyers who assure an unfamiliar foreign client that it has an excellent case before examining the contract, the other side's likely evidence, and the defendant's assets. If the proposed local counsel cannot explain what might defeat the claim or make it uneconomic, I keep looking.
Yes, if the court has subject-matter jurisdiction, venue is proper, and there is a valid basis for personal jurisdiction over the defendant. The defendant's U.S. contacts or agreement to litigate here often matter. American assets can help with collection but do not, by themselves, establish personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. If the assets are overseas, enforcement ordinarily requires a separate recognition proceeding.
Neither is better across the board. Arbitration offers an enforcement advantage when the debtor has assets in several countries because of the New York Convention. It also brings institutional and arbitrator fees and limited opportunities to challenge an award. When a Chinese manufacturer and its assets are in China, we often prefer litigation in the right Chinese court.
An emergency asset freeze can come within days in some courts, as it did in our mold case. A decision on the merits, an appeal, and actual collection take longer, particularly when enforcement requires proceedings in another country. Ask foreign counsel for separate estimates for each stage.
Our usual screening threshold for straightforward litigation or arbitration in China is about $350,000. Below that, we generally advise against routine money claims because legal costs consume too much of the likely recovery. Chinese law sets no such minimum. Smaller claims involving essential tooling or injunctive relief can justify litigation, while much larger claims against defendants with no reachable assets may not.
State ownership does not necessarily confer sovereign immunity. Depending on the entity and claim, immunity statutes or treaties may apply. Immunity from suit and immunity from enforcement are separate questions, and a waiver permitting litigation does not necessarily authorize attachment of government property. Before filing, determine the entity's legal status, the nature of the transaction, and which assets can lawfully be reached.
Yes, particularly when multiple companies are involved or contracts contain inconsistent dispute resolution provisions. Parallel proceedings increase expense and the risk of conflicting orders. Rules concerning stays, parallel proceedings, and the effect of earlier decisions vary by jurisdiction. We coordinate filings with local counsel so that a move in one country does not undermine the case elsewhere.
The governing language clause and the original contract text matter. A Chinese court will not necessarily rely on an English summary, and other courts may require sworn translations or specific authentication procedures. Translation can add material cost in an arbitration or a document-heavy case, and poor translations can change the apparent meaning of contractual obligations. Preserve the originals and have lawyers who understand the relevant language review key provisions before filing.
Fee recovery depends on the governing law, the contract, and the forum. American litigation normally follows the American rule, subject to statutory, contractual, and other exceptions. Some foreign courts award specified costs, and arbitral tribunals may allocate costs under the agreement and applicable rules. Even an award of legal fees must be collected. Budget on the assumption that you will have to pay your own lawyers.
If your company has a dispute with a foreign manufacturer, distributor, customer, or business partner, contact our International Dispute Resolution Team. Send us the contract, a short explanation of the problem, the countries involved, the amount at stake, and any approaching deadlines or immediate concerns about assets or evidence. We can assess whether pursuing the claim makes economic sense and what it is likely to cost.

Choosing New York law in an English-language contract does not, by itself, give a New York court jurisdiction over every foreign defendant.

We have reviewed contracts that make an ordinary claim extraordinarily expensive to pursue. One agreement with a Chinese company required negotiation, followed by in-person mediation in China, followed by Chinese-language arbitration before three arbitrators, and the arbitrator-selection procedure was unclear as well. A straightforward payment claim under that agreement faced an expensive procedural path before anyone reached the merits.

I ordinarily remove mandatory negotiation and mediation requirements from our international contracts. Parties can negotiate or mediate whenever they wish, and we often recommend it. Mandatory steps give a party looking to delay another argument about why the case cannot proceed, sometimes while it moves assets. Carefully defined escalation procedures make sense in some transactions, but I do not insert them as boilerplate. We generally settle the dispute resolution clause near the end of contract drafting, after we understand the likely breaches, remedies, parties, and assets. Our article on Drafting China Dispute Resolution Clauses that Work discusses an actual contract illustrating the problem.

An unsigned or missing agreement complicates the forum question but does not necessarily defeat the claim. Purchase orders, payments, emails, and performance may establish a contract under the applicable law. The parties can still dispute whether an arbitration clause was accepted or a court has jurisdiction. Without an enforceable arbitration agreement, neither side can ordinarily force arbitration simply because it now prefers that forum. This is one reason the documents are the international deal.

Suing a Foreign Company in the United States

To sue a foreign company in the United States, a plaintiff needs subject-matter jurisdiction, proper venue, and a valid basis for personal jurisdiction over the defendant. That basis may come from the defendant's relevant contacts with a state, its agreement to litigate there, or an applicable federal jurisdictional provision. American assets can help with collection, but owning them does not, by itself, establish personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. These questions need answers before filing.

American discovery attracts plaintiffs to U.S. courts, but obtaining evidence overseas can be difficult. Documents held by American banks and business partners may be accessible. Compelling testimony or records from a mainland Chinese company is another matter. China's evidence-gathering and data laws can restrict collection and transmission, and a U.S. subpoena is not directly enforceable in China. Before choosing an American forum, determine where the critical evidence is and whether you can obtain it.

Mainland China is a party to the Hague Service Convention and objects to the methods in Article 10, including postal service. When the Convention applies, service must follow a permitted method. For mainland Chinese defendants with known addresses, we generally recommend formal Hague service through the proper Convention channel, especially when the client may later seek recognition of the judgment in China. Service through China's Central Authority can take months and requires careful preparation, including translation.

Two recent federal appellate decisions make email service on defendants in China particularly risky. In Smart Study Co. v. Shenzhenshixindajixieyouxiangongsi, decided in December 2025, the Second Circuit held that the Hague Service Convention prohibited email service on the China-based defendants in that case. The Seventh Circuit adopted the same treaty interpretation in Kangol LLC v. Hangzhou Chuanyue Silk Import & Export Co. in May 2026, but remanded to determine whether the Convention applied given the dispute over the defendant's address. The defendant's actual location and the Convention's scope still matter. A quick default judgment obtained through questionable service is a poor bargain if it cannot later be enforced.

Suing in the Foreign Company's Home Country

Suing in the defendant's home country can avoid a separate judgment-recognition proceeding when the local court can reach its assets. The challenge is local procedure. A case built around American depositions needs a different evidentiary approach in a court that relies mainly on documents.

For China manufacturing disputes, we often favor litigation in the right Chinese court when the defendant and its assets are in China. That court can enforce locally without first requiring recognition of an American judgment. Our experience with ordinary business disputes in major Chinese commercial centers has generally been favorable, though cases involving important local employers or politically sensitive interests require more caution.

Chinese courts can order property preservation when the applicable standards are met. A sensible contractual damages clause helps define the claim and can support a preservation application, but it does not automatically entitle the plaintiff to a bank freeze. The court decides whether to grant relief and may require security. Chinese manufacturers generally know that these clauses can lead to a frozen bank account, which makes a good damages provision one of the best ways to get a factory to honor its contract in the first place.

Under the revised Chinese Arbitration Law, effective March 1, 2026, arbitral tribunals seated in mainland China still cannot themselves freeze bank accounts. In qualifying arbitrations, parties can seek court-ordered property preservation, and the revised law also permits applications to a court in urgent situations before arbitration begins. We consider those remedies even when the contract requires arbitration.

CIETAC can be an excellent choice when a state-owned company insists on arbitration or there are reasons to avoid the defendant's local court. In a small city where the defendant is a major employer or taxpayer, properly structured arbitration may reduce concerns about local influence over the merits. The arbitral institution, seat, and available court assistance still matter.

When a dispute belongs in a Chinese court, we work with Chinese litigators we know. A foreign company hiring a Chinese law firm directly is almost always a mistake, because few foreign companies know China well enough to pick the right firm or to work with one on their own. International counsel helps select local lawyers, coordinate evidence and strategy, and keep the client informed about costs and risks. We take the same approach elsewhere, looking for lawyers who actually litigate in the relevant courts. A firm's claim that it handles international matters tells us little about its courtroom experience.

When International Arbitration Makes Sense

Arbitration has a genuine enforcement advantage when the debtor has assets in several countries. The New York Convention provides a system for recognizing and enforcing qualifying awards in more than 170 jurisdictions. It permits specified defenses to enforcement, but courts ordinarily do not retry the merits. No comparable worldwide system exists for ordinary foreign court judgments.

Arbitration can be expensive. Parties usually pay their lawyers, the administering institution, and the arbitrators. Three-member tribunals, experts, witnesses from different countries, translation, and hearings can push a substantial case into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Challenges to arbitral awards are tightly limited, and the losing party has little opportunity to correct an error.

As we discuss in our article on international arbitration in cross-border contracts, a contract binds only the parties covered by its arbitration agreement, subject to recognized rules concerning non-signatories. A dispute involving several affiliates and contracts can become procedurally difficult when only some parties agreed to arbitrate. Emergency arbitrators and court-assisted interim relief are available in certain arbitrations, but the powers and procedures vary.

When Negotiation or Mediation Makes Sense

Settlement becomes possible when the other side has a reason to make a deal. A supplier may want future orders. A debtor whose bank accounts have been frozen wants access to its money. Before negotiating, I want to know what the other side needs and what it can deliver. Repeating that our client has a strong case does little when the defendant thinks it can ignore us.

Mediation can work even in very large disputes. Our firm represented the Government of Haiti in a dispute with a Chinese construction company that ended in a private mediation settlement of nearly $35 million after approximately two years. Keep watching limitation periods and other deadlines while negotiations or mediation continue, and do not assume the discussions suspend them.

A settlement needs to be enforceable where performance is expected. Identify the actual obligated entity and any guarantors, address payment security and installments, and specify when claims are released. If a Chinese company is paying money or releasing goods in China, we usually want a Chinese-language agreement that works under Chinese law and before the likely enforcement court. In one cross-border credit dispute we wrote about, incomplete settlement documents helped turn an apparent resolution into further litigation.

Getting Paid After a Judgment or Arbitration Award

A U.S. judgment ordinarily must be recognized under the law of the foreign country before the creditor can use local enforcement procedures. The defendant may raise objections concerning jurisdiction, service, finality, or public policy. Collection is then governed by the law where the assets are located. A creditor cannot simply present an American judgment to a foreign bank and demand payment.

Chinese courts have become more receptive to recognizing certain American judgments under an evolving reciprocity framework. Enforcement is not automatic. Jurisdiction, service, and the judgment's eligibility under current Chinese law all require careful review by Chinese counsel.

Arbitral awards ordinarily follow a different recognition framework, including the New York Convention where applicable. Even after recognition, the creditor needs assets it can lawfully reach. I reassess the economics before filing and whenever the next stage, including enforcement, requires substantial expense.

When a Foreign Supplier Dispute Involves Fraud

In a Yiwu supplier fraud matter, a buyer paid about $177,000 to a Chinese intermediary for three shipments. The first, worth approximately $35,000, arrived. The other goods never left China. According to the buyer, the intermediary passed only a small portion of the payment to the manufacturer, then spent months claiming that goods were nearly finished or had shipped. The buyer even sent representatives to investigate, but the promised deliveries never materialized.

We recommended that the buyer retain a reputable Chinese lawyer experienced in economic-crime complaints to evaluate a police referral. The alleged failure to fund production, coupled with false shipment claims, warranted examining whether the conduct was intentional fraud. We could not promise the police would accept the case, because Chinese authorities can treat a failed commercial transaction as a civil dispute.

Do not threaten criminal prosecution to collect an ordinary commercial debt. That can create legal problems of its own. When the evidence genuinely suggests fraud, counsel should evaluate criminal reporting alongside the civil claims and deadlines. Banks, payment platforms, insurers, and marketplaces may also offer recovery options worth investigating before financing an international lawsuit.

Defending Against Foreign Lawsuits and Judgments

Companies sometimes disregard a foreign court summons because they have no operations in the country, believe the plaintiff is bluffing, or think a judgment issued there cannot affect them. An arbitration notice can be dismissed just as casually. That is a serious gamble. A foreign court may proceed to a default judgment, and an arbitral tribunal can issue an award when a properly notified respondent refuses to participate. The plaintiff may later attempt enforcement wherever the defendant has assets.

When foreign legal papers arrive, preserve the record and have counsel calculate the response deadline immediately. The first review should cover jurisdiction, service or arbitral notice, contractual forum requirements, and whether an appearance or objection affects available defenses. Check insurance and indemnification rights, related proceedings, and possible counterclaims. An ill-considered response can waive defenses that would otherwise remain available.

We also defend companies and owners when foreign creditors seek recognition of judgments in the United States. Recognition of foreign-country money judgments here is primarily governed by state law, often through a version of the Uniform Foreign-Country Money Judgments Recognition Act. The creditor ordinarily has to establish that the judgment qualifies for recognition, and the debtor can raise permitted defenses, including jurisdictional or serious notice and due-process defects. A U.S. court does not normally reopen the foreign case just because the debtor thinks the foreign judge got the facts wrong.

These cases often turn on old records: who was served, whether the defendant appeared, whether it objected to jurisdiction, and what happened in the foreign proceeding. The defense must fit the recognition law of the U.S. state where the creditor filed. We represent both sides of these disputes, and our article on enforcing or challenging foreign judgments in the United States explains the available objections.

The Questions I Ask Before Hiring Foreign Litigation Counsel

Some years ago, I came across an email from one of our international litigators to a client considering a lawsuit in a small emerging-market country. The client wanted to know whether the claim was worth pursuing and which local firm to hire. Our lawyer had listed the questions we planned to ask the firms under consideration. I still use much the same list today.

  1. Which court has jurisdiction, and does a forum clause or arbitration agreement change that? Could another country also hear the dispute?
  2. Would a judge, jury, or panel decide the case, and how experienced are they with disputes involving foreign companies?
  3. What evidence will the court accept, what authentication or translation is required, and how much weight does it give live testimony?
  4. Can we compel documents or testimony from the defendant or third parties? Are pretrial depositions or other discovery procedures available?
  5. Can the court resolve weak claims or defenses before a full trial?
  6. Is corruption a credible concern in this court? Does the opposing party have political or economic influence, and are foreign litigants treated fairly?
  7. Can we freeze assets, obtain an injunction, preserve evidence, or secure goods? What proof or security is required?
  8. What will each stage cost, including court fees, lawyers, experts, translation, travel, security, appeals, and enforcement? Give us a realistic range, not an optimistic estimate.
  9. Can the winner recover legal fees or costs? Which expenses qualify, and are contingency or alternative fee arrangements permitted?
  10. How long do emergency relief, the first decision, appeals, and collection typically take? What causes delays?
  11. When do comparable cases settle, and what usually brings the defendant to the table?
  12. What defenses, counterclaims, or weaknesses in our documents and conduct concern you most? What have we overlooked?
  13. Where are the defendant's assets, how can we investigate them before filing, and how effective is collection in this jurisdiction?
  14. Who will actually handle the case? How much of the firm's practice is litigation, how often does it represent foreign clients, and what happened in comparable cases?
  15. What would make you advise us not to sue? What is the worst likely outcome, what are the realistic collection prospects, and is the case worth the money?

That last question matters most to me. I distrust lawyers who assure an unfamiliar foreign client that it has an excellent case before examining the contract, the other side's likely evidence, and the defendant's assets. If the proposed local counsel cannot explain what might defeat the claim or make it uneconomic, I keep looking.

Frequently Asked Questions About International Commercial Disputes

Can my company sue a foreign company in the United States?

Yes, if the court has subject-matter jurisdiction, venue is proper, and there is a valid basis for personal jurisdiction over the defendant. The defendant's U.S. contacts or agreement to litigate here often matter. American assets can help with collection but do not, by themselves, establish personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. If the assets are overseas, enforcement ordinarily requires a separate recognition proceeding.

Is international arbitration better than suing in court?

Neither is better across the board. Arbitration offers an enforcement advantage when the debtor has assets in several countries because of the New York Convention. It also brings institutional and arbitrator fees and limited opportunities to challenge an award. When a Chinese manufacturer and its assets are in China, we often prefer litigation in the right Chinese court.

How long does an international commercial dispute take?

An emergency asset freeze can come within days in some courts, as it did in our mold case. A decision on the merits, an appeal, and actual collection take longer, particularly when enforcement requires proceedings in another country. Ask foreign counsel for separate estimates for each stage.

What size dispute is worth pursuing?

Our usual screening threshold for straightforward litigation or arbitration in China is about $350,000. Below that, we generally advise against routine money claims because legal costs consume too much of the likely recovery. Chinese law sets no such minimum. Smaller claims involving essential tooling or injunctive relief can justify litigation, while much larger claims against defendants with no reachable assets may not.

What if a government-owned foreign company owes us money?

State ownership does not necessarily confer sovereign immunity. Depending on the entity and claim, immunity statutes or treaties may apply. Immunity from suit and immunity from enforcement are separate questions, and a waiver permitting litigation does not necessarily authorize attachment of government property. Before filing, determine the entity's legal status, the nature of the transaction, and which assets can lawfully be reached.

Can lawsuits or arbitrations proceed in more than one country?

Yes, particularly when multiple companies are involved or contracts contain inconsistent dispute resolution provisions. Parallel proceedings increase expense and the risk of conflicting orders. Rules concerning stays, parallel proceedings, and the effect of earlier decisions vary by jurisdiction. We coordinate filings with local counsel so that a move in one country does not undermine the case elsewhere.

What if our evidence or contract is in another language?

The governing language clause and the original contract text matter. A Chinese court will not necessarily rely on an English summary, and other courts may require sworn translations or specific authentication procedures. Translation can add material cost in an arbitration or a document-heavy case, and poor translations can change the apparent meaning of contractual obligations. Preserve the originals and have lawyers who understand the relevant language review key provisions before filing.

Can we recover legal fees if we win?

Fee recovery depends on the governing law, the contract, and the forum. American litigation normally follows the American rule, subject to statutory, contractual, and other exceptions. Some foreign courts award specified costs, and arbitral tribunals may allocate costs under the agreement and applicable rules. Even an award of legal fees must be collected. Budget on the assumption that you will have to pay your own lawyers.

Getting an International Dispute Evaluated

If your company has a dispute with a foreign manufacturer, distributor, customer, or business partner, contact our International Dispute Resolution Team. Send us the contract, a short explanation of the problem, the countries involved, the amount at stake, and any approaching deadlines or immediate concerns about assets or evidence. We can assess whether pursuing the claim makes economic sense and what it is likely to cost.
