Reviewing them will not make them suitable China contracts. Starting with a contract drafted for the transaction and jurisdiction is usually more efficient. See China Manufacturing Contracts: Why Your Draft Does Not Work.

Companies also overspend on trade secret programs and foreign patents. A company with little valuable confidential information should question the need for an elaborate trade secret program. A startup should have a business reason before pursuing patents in numerous countries. Be skeptical of lawyers who recommend every available remedy without discussing its cost and likely value.

Choosing an IP Lawyer Who Understands Your Business

IP lawyers have different specialties. A patent lawyer who excels at pharmaceutical patents may have little experience negotiating Chinese manufacturing agreements. An international business lawyer experienced in trademarks and contracts should not prosecute complicated software patents. Trademark registration and trademark litigation also require different skills.

Firm size tells you little about whether a lawyer can handle your matter. A small IP boutique may be best for specialized patent work, and a solo practitioner can be excellent for routine filings. Foreign manufacturing, distribution, and licensing matters often call for international business experience. Our article, The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes, describes what can happen when companies hire lawyers without the necessary experience.

At Harris Sliwoski, much of our international IP practice involves protecting companies before they work with foreign businesses and helping them when those relationships go wrong. We have seen companies register trademarks while overlooking tooling ownership and sign confidentiality agreements that do nothing to prevent manufacturers from competing with them. Those experiences inform our advice about where clients should spend their legal budgets.

Questions to Ask Before Hiring an IP Lawyer

Spend less time asking how long a lawyer has practiced and more time asking how that lawyer would approach your business. My favorite question is "What would you protect first if this were your company?" Then ask why. A lawyer who recommends five trademark applications, two contracts, and an international patent strategy before learning about your business deserves skepticism.

I would also ask:

  • Have you handled this problem before? Request examples involving similar products, industries, or jurisdictions.
  • What would you tell us not to buy? The answer helps distinguish judgment from salesmanship.
  • How is our IP protection most likely to fail? This reveals whether the lawyer understands real disputes.
  • Who will handle our work? Determine who makes the important decisions and who performs the work.
  • What will we have when the work is finished? An application, registration, signed contract, and enforceable legal right are different things.
  • What will it cost if something goes wrong? Ask about refusals, oppositions, breaches, and enforcement.

A good lawyer should answer in language you understand. If you leave the consultation unsure what the lawyer proposes or why you need it, keep asking before hiring.

How IP Legal Fees Work

IP legal services are sold under several pricing arrangements. Routine filings and some contracts work well with flat fees. Litigation and complicated advisory work usually require hourly or phased billing. Monthly fixed fees sometimes make sense for ongoing portfolio management.

Fee structure Typical work Questions to ask
Flat fee Trademark filings, copyright registrations, standard agreements What is included, and what costs extra?
Hourly Litigation, complex licensing, specialized advice What is the estimated total cost, and when will it be updated?
Phased project fee IP audits, multi-country filings, complex transactions What does each phase deliver?
Monthly fixed fee Ongoing portfolio management and advice What services are included and excluded?

A Lower Quote Is Not Always a Better Deal

Suppose one firm quotes $1,000 for a trademark application and another quotes $2,000. The cheaper quote excludes clearance searches, government fees, and nearly all post-filing work, while the higher quote includes some or all of those services. Or perhaps only one firm understands which trademark classes cover your products. Remember the protective-glove company: it paid for a trademark registration without getting the protection it needed. A less expensive lawyer may lack the experience to distinguish what you need from what you don't, or may be more interested in generating fees than saving you money. You could end up paying for 11 trademark applications when one would have protected your business just as well.

Patent estimates require particular care. The initial filing cost does not tell you what you will spend responding to examiner objections, filing abroad, or maintaining issued patents. Find out which stages each estimate covers.

Your engagement agreement should say exactly what you are buying. For trademarks, identify the marks, jurisdictions, classes, clearance searches, and government fees. Specify whether office action responses are included and what happens if someone opposes the application.

For manufacturing contracts, establish which agreements the firm will prepare, whether manufacturer verification is included, what languages will be used, which version controls, and whether the fee covers negotiations and revisions. Ask how the agreement will be made enforceable where the manufacturer operates.

The same principles apply to patents, IP ownership reviews, licensing, and litigation. Define the deliverables, your responsibilities, and the additional work requiring your approval. Distinguish the lawyer's preparation time from government processing time. A firm can file a trademark application promptly without controlling when or whether it is approved.

Agree in advance how unexpected work will be billed, including trademark conflicts, patent examiner rejections, and substantial contract revisions. Competent lawyers should be comfortable discussing these issues before starting. Before signing, make sure you understand what the firm will do, why your business needs it, what you will receive, and what you will pay. Resolve anything unclear before authorizing the work.
